name: b01-priority-ladder
title: Which assignment wins: the priority ladder
spec: A vertical ladder of four horizontal bars from low priority at the bottom to high at the top, labelled with numbers on the left side: 0 at the bottom, then 250, then 500, then 750, then 1000 at the top. Bar at 250 labelled: a category (fixed 250). Bar at 500 labelled: a configuration overlay (default 500, range 0 to 1000). Bar at 750 labelled: a node (fixed 750). A small grey note beside the 250 and 750 rungs: 250 and 750 are reserved, an overlay may not use them. A small label at the very top: -1 means the overlay is ignored. Orange arrow pointing up beside the top rung labelled: the highest number wins.
anchor: ### 3.6 Configuration overlays
alt: The priority ladder for role assignments
cap: Role priority: a node beats an overlay, and an overlay beats a category, because the highest number wins.

name: b01-reconcile-loop
title: How CMDaemon turns database state into Linux files
spec: A left-to-right flow of five boxes with arrows between them, read in time order with number circles 1 to 5. Box 1: You change an object and run commit in cmsh or click Save in Base View. Box 2: CMDaemon evaluates the inheritance rules across partitions, categories, overlays and devices. Box 3: CMDaemon regenerates the affected daemon configuration files on the head node. Box 4: CMDaemon pushes state to regular node CMDaemon instances over TCP port 8081. Box 5: The Linux service behind the file is reloaded or signalled, such as dhcpd, named, nfs-server or slurmctld. Under box 3, a small monospace note chip: This file was automatically generated by cmd. Do not edit manually! Orange arrow or note on box 3: a hand edit to this file is overwritten. Under box 5 a separate note: the service reads its file once at start or on a signal, so the reload makes the new value active.
anchor: ### 7.1 Mental model: How CMDaemon reconciles database state into Linux files
alt: The CMDaemon reconciliation loop
cap: Reconciliation: CMDaemon regenerates files from the database and reloads the service, so hand edits to generated files do not last.

name: b02-ip-offset
title: Why the BMC needs an IP offset
spec: Two horizontal rows of address boxes sharing one network, 10.141.0.0/16. Top row labelled boot interface (BOOTIF) with ten small boxes 10.141.0.1 to 10.141.0.10. Bottom row labelled bmc interface with offset 0.0.0.20 with ten small boxes 10.141.0.21 to 10.141.0.30. A green bracket or gap between the two rows, with the note: the offset moves the BMC sequence along the block so no address is claimed twice. Beside the first row a grey note: without the offset, both sequences start at .1 and collide on every address. Orange highlight on the gap between the two rows. Monospace for the addresses and the offset value.
anchor: ## 4. Names and addresses
alt: Boot and BMC address ranges with an offset
cap: IP offset: the BMC addresses start after the boot addresses, so the two interfaces never share an address.

name: b02-burn-split
title: How a burn run uses the pre-install and post-install phases
spec: A left-to-right flow of four steps with number circles 1 to 4 and arrows between them. Step 1: burn --config <name> -n node001..node064 start, reboot the node into the node-installer environment (RAM-based). Step 2: run every pre-install phase, destructive block-level disk and memory tests allowed, local drives not mounted as a root filesystem. Step 3: all pre-install phases pass, provision the full software image onto disk and boot the production kernel. Step 4: run every post-install phase with full driver support, examples hpl, GPU DCGM stress tests, InfiniBand bandwidth checks. Above step 4, a side container labelled stress phase with two parallel boxes: a timed stress test (hpl or memtester) and, beside it, a monitor marked endless equals 1 (mce_check, kmon), with the note: monitors stop when the last non-endless test in the phase finishes. Orange note on step 2: destructive tests are safe here because no running OS is on the drives.
anchor: ### 10.2 Designing a production burn-in gate with `burnconfigs`
alt: The pre-install and post-install burn phases
cap: Burn-in order: destructive tests run in the RAM-based installer before the image is provisioned, then full-stack tests run on the production kernel.

name: b03-gateway-order
title: Where a node's default gateway comes from
spec: A vertical decision chain of three boxes with arrows going down, each box a yes or no question with the answer on the side. Box 1: Does the category set a default gateway? Yes arrow goes right to a green end box: use the category gateway. No arrow goes down to Box 2: Does the network object have a gateway? Yes arrow goes right to a green end box: use the network gateway. No arrow goes down to Box 3: Is the gateway 0.0.0.0? Yes arrow goes right to an orange end box: DHCP on the head node hands out 10.141.255.254, the head node alias. Monospace for 0.0.0.0 and 10.141.255.254. Small note under the chain: the order is set by the code in bcm_netconf.default_gateway.
anchor: ### Four places an internal-network value can come from
alt: The order for choosing a default gateway
cap: Default gateway: the category wins, then the network gateway, and a 0.0.0.0 gateway falls back to the head node alias.

name: b03-mig-budget
title: Why an over-long MIG profile list silently drops slices
spec: Two horizontal bars of seven equal slots each, labelled GPU slices 1 to 7 along the top. Upper bar, labelled 5*1g.5gb,2g.10gb: five small slots marked 1g.5gb and then one wide slot spanning two slots marked 2g.10gb, all seven filled, green, with a tick and the text: fits, 7 of 7 slices. Lower bar, labelled 6*1g.5gb,2g.10gb: six small slots marked 1g.5gb filled green, then the seventh slot filled, and the 2g.10gb entry shown as a dashed grey outline sticking out past the end of the bar, with the note: needs 2 more slices, left unallocated, no error shown. Orange highlight on the dashed part. Monospace for the profile strings and the profile names.
anchor: ## 7. GPU settings (3.17)
alt: Slice budget for MIG profile lists
cap: MIG budget: a profile list needing more than seven GPU slices quietly loses the entries that do not fit.

name: b03-beyond-cmdaemon
title: The order of preference for going beyond CMDaemon
spec: A staircase of six steps rising from bottom left to top right, numbered 1 to 6 with number circles, each step a box with a title and one short line. Step 1 (bottom, green): Configure through CMDaemon in cmsh or Base View, CMDaemon tracks the state. Step 2: Use a different image for a category or a node. Step 3: Place files through the image. Step 4: Use FrozenFile to stop CMDaemon rewriting a file. Step 5: Use initialize and finalize scripts, which run at the initrd stage. Step 6 (top, orange): Use a shared directory for the software the nodes run. Left side arrow pointing up labelled: more of your own tracking at each step. Monospace for FrozenFile, initialize and finalize.
anchor: ## 8. Going beyond CMDaemon: the manual's order of preference
alt: Six ways to go beyond CMDaemon in order
cap: Beyond CMDaemon: start with CMDaemon settings and move down the list only when none fits, since each step adds your own tracking.

name: b04-provisioners
title: Provisioning nodes and node groups
spec: A top box labelled Head node with the note: the head node always has the provisioning role. Below it, a row of two provisioning node boxes labelled Provisioning node A and Provisioning node B, each with a small label provisioningslots 10 (default). Under Provisioning node A a box for nodegroups rack-a with three small node boxes labelled rack-a nodes. Under Provisioning node B a box for nodegroups rack-b with three small node boxes labelled rack-b nodes. A grey box at the far right labelled nodes in no group, with an arrow to the provisioner that has no nodegroups (the head node). Arrows from the head node down to the two provisioners are dashed, labelled provisioning image traffic. Note at the bottom: a node in a group uses only provisioners that list that group. Orange highlight on the rack-b path. Monospace for provisioningslots and nodegroups.
anchor: ## 6. Scaling provisioning: provisioning nodes (5.2)
alt: Provisioning nodes split by node group
cap: Provisioning nodes: each node group pulls images only from the provisioners that list that group.

name: b04-kernelmodule-replace
title: A lower kernel-module list replaces the higher one
spec: Three stacked boxes, top to bottom: Software image (kernelmodules list), Category (kernelmodules list), Node (kernelmodules list). Between each pair of boxes a downward arrow labelled overrides. Beside the Node box, a note: a lower level replaces the higher level completely, it does not add to it. Left of the stack, a grey crossed-out box: appending to the image list from the node. Orange highlight on the node box with the text: an incomplete list here drops the image's storage and network drivers. Under the stack a green box: change the list on the image, then createramdisk rebuilds the ramdisk. Monospace for kernelmodules and createramdisk.
anchor: ## 7. Software images and kernels (5.3, chapter 9)
alt: Kernel module lists replace each other by level
cap: Kernel modules: a lower level replaces the higher list, so set the list on the image and rebuild the ramdisk.

name: b04-imageupdate-flow
title: Safe live update of a running node
spec: A left-to-right flow of four steps with number circles 1 to 4 and arrows between them. Step 1: updateprovisioners, push the new image to the provisioners first. Step 2: imageupdate -n node001, a dry run that writes nothing by default, then read the result with synclog. Step 3: for a larger change, a side branch arrow to a grey box: reboot instead, which does an AUTO install of the latest image. Step 4: imageupdate -n node001 -w, applies the change to the running node. Orange highlight on step 4 with the note: -w is the switch that makes the change real. Monospace for the commands.
anchor: ## 8. Updating a running node: `imageupdate` and exclude lists (5.6)
alt: Dry run then apply for a live image update
cap: Live update: push the image to the provisioners, dry run imageupdate, read synclog, and only then apply with the -w flag.

name: b05-commit-cycle
title: The cmsh commit cycle
spec: A left-to-right flow with three boxes and a decision. Box 1: Make the change locally with set, add, clear, append, removefrom or remove. Note under box 1: nothing reaches CMDaemon yet, the prompt shows asterisks. Box 2: modified, lists objects with uncommitted changes: + new, - to be removed, blank changed. Diamond: Does the list look right? No arrow goes down to a grey box: refresh, which undoes the local changes. Yes arrow goes right to Box 3: commit, sends the changes to CMDaemon. Under box 3, a green note: commit -w waits for background work such as cloning an image. Orange highlight on box 2 with the note: check modified before every commit. Small warning under the commit box: a commit also runs any pending remove, even one queued in another mode. Monospace for the commands.
anchor: ## 5. The commit model: the habit that matters most
alt: The cmsh change, check and commit cycle
cap: Commit cycle: stage the change, check modified, then commit, or refresh to throw the staged change away.

name: b06-directory-options
title: Three ways to get POSIX users onto the cluster
spec: Three side-by-side columns, each a panel with a title and a small diagram. Column 1 titled 1. BCM standalone OpenLDAP (default): one box Head node OpenLDAP as the primary authority, with an arrow to a row of compute node boxes, label cmsh user and group modes manage users. Column 2 titled 2. Direct external LDAP or AD: a box Corporate LDAP or Active Directory on the far side, with arrows going straight to compute and login node boxes, labelled sssd or nslcd on each node, no head node in the lookup path. Column 3 titled 3. OpenLDAP syncrepl consumer on head node: a box Corporate LDAP as provider, a dashed arrow labelled syncrepl rid=2 to the head node OpenLDAP replica, then arrows from the head node to compute nodes, labelled local UID lookups. Orange highlight on column 3 with the note: lookups stay inside the cluster. Monospace for sssd.conf, nslcd, syncrepl and rid=2.
anchor: ### 9.2 Enterprise identity architectures: Local LDAP vs Direct External LDAP vs `syncrepl`
alt: Three directory architectures for cluster users
cap: Directory options: the local LDAP is simplest, direct external LDAP centralises users, and syncrepl keeps job lookups local.

name: b06-rotation-order
title: Order of steps for a full credential rotation
spec: A vertical sequence of four boxes with downward arrows and number circles 1 to 4. Box 1: Revoke or expire the management certificate in cert mode, the access someone may be using right now (highlight in orange). Box 2: Rotate the four core passwords with cm-change-passwd, on the active head node and then the passive head node, then push the new image hash to nodes with updateprovisioners and imageupdate -w. Box 3: Rotate the OpenLDAP root password if directory administration was exposed, follow Appendix I (note: cm-change-passwd does not touch it). Box 4: Rotate the out-of-band BMC passwords with bmcsettings, commit, then check credentialsoverview --inverse for outliers. Right side note: work top to bottom, closing the live door first. Monospace for the commands.
anchor: ### 9.4 Step-by-step incident response: Revoking compromised credentials and rotating cluster secrets
alt: Four-step credential rotation order
cap: Rotation order: revoke live access first, then the four admin passwords, the LDAP root password, and the BMC credentials.

name: b06-login-boundaries
title: Three places that enforce the login boundary
spec: Three stacked horizontal bands, each a panel with a machine name and a lock icon. Band 1: Head node, edit /etc/ssh/sshd_config, AllowUsers root or AllowGroups, PasswordAuthentication no. Band 2: Regular GPU compute nodes, set usernodelogin onlywhenjob on compute categories, with a note: a researcher can SSH to the node only while holding an active Slurm job on it, via pam_bright.so. Band 3: Dedicated login nodes, set usernodelogin always in a login category, with cgroup or limits.conf resource limits and no route to bmcnet 10.148.0.0/16. Orange highlight on band 2. Monospace for the file path, the setting values, pam_bright.so and 10.148.0.0/16.
anchor: ### 9.5 Hardening SSH and login-node boundaries (`usernodelogin` and `AllowUsers`)
alt: Login boundaries on head, compute and login nodes
cap: Login boundaries: the head node, compute nodes and login nodes each have their own SSH rule.

name: b07-power-waves
title: How a batch power-on spreads over time
spec: A horizontal timeline axis labelled seconds with tick marks at 0, 20, 40 and 60. Four waves stacked as rows or groups, each a row of three small rack boxes labelled rack01 to rack12 across the four waves. Wave 1 starts at 0 s with racks 1 to 3, wave 2 at 20 s with racks 4 to 6, wave 3 at 40 s with racks 7 to 9, wave 4 at 60 s with racks 10 to 12. Between racks inside a wave, no gap (started together). Label on the arrows between waves: parallel-delay 20 s. Title note: power on -p 3 rack[01-12]. Orange highlight on the first wave with the note: each wave is one more group of racks drawing inrush current at once. A small grey note: count the waves before you run the command. Monospace for the command and the tick values.
anchor: ## 3. Power operations (4.2)
alt: Batch power-on waves over time
cap: Batch power-on: racks start in waves three at a time, spaced 20 seconds apart, to limit the inrush current.

name: b07-firmware-activation
title: Why a firmware update is not active until the AC power cycle
spec: A left-to-right flow of five state boxes with arrows, each box a state name with the result text. Box 1: flashing, with a progress percentage. Box 2: pending, Result column: success: AC power cycle to activate. Box 3 (orange, the key step): AC power cycle, cut all AC inputs, for example a PDU that turns the system off or pulling every mains lead. Box 4: firmware status again, State shows completed with Result success: activated. Box 5: new version shown, for example 96.00.70.00.01 to 96.00.74.00.01. Below the arrow from box 2 to box 3, a grey crossed-out side path labelled power reset, which is only a DC board reset and does not activate some components. Monospace for firmware status, firmware flash, power reset and the version strings.
anchor: ## 7. Firmware (14.5.3)
alt: Firmware states from flashing to activated
cap: Firmware activation: the update stays pending until a true AC power cycle, because a power reset does not activate it.

name: b07-sol-layers
title: Three layers that must match for serial over LAN
spec: Three stacked horizontal layers, a stack of three wide panels with a lock icon at the left of each. Top panel: The BMC BIOS, SOL enabled with matching speed, flow control and port. Middle panel: The node kernel, set through the software image, set enablesol yes. Bottom panel: The node BIOS, serial port enabled with the same settings. Arrows or bracket on the right side labelled: all three must use the same key, a mismatch gives a garbled or silent console. Below the stack, a green box: 115200 bps, flow control on, ttyS0 on x86_64 or ttyAMA0 on aarch64. Orange highlight on the middle panel. Monospace for enablesol, 115200, ttyS0 and ttyAMA0.
anchor: ## 8. Serial over LAN (14.7)
alt: Three layers that must agree for serial over LAN
cap: Serial over LAN: the BMC BIOS, the node kernel and the node BIOS must all use the same serial settings.

name: b08-slurm-takeover
title: Slurm controller takeover on a head-node failover
spec: A left-to-right flow of four boxes with arrows. Box 1: Active head node fails, the passive head node takes over the cluster services. Box 2: cmha makeactive runs through CMDaemon. Box 3: The pre-failover script slurm.takeover.sh runs scontrol takeover, the backup slurmctld takes over without a break. Box 4: Primary head restarts later, the primary slurmctld takes its role back. A side box above Box 3 labelled slurmctldstartpolicy TAKEOVER, with a note: stops BCM restarting the stopped primary slurmctld right away, which would undo the takeover. Under the flow, a grey note: a single slurmctld uses ALWAYS. Orange highlight on the TAKEOVER side box. Monospace for cmha makeactive, slurm.takeover.sh, scontrol takeover, slurmctldstartpolicy and TAKEOVER.
anchor: ## 7. High availability (7.2.4)
alt: Slurm controller takeover during head-node failover
cap: Slurm takeover: the backup controller takes over through a script, and the TAKEOVER policy stops BCM undoing it.

name: b08-prejob-guard
title: How a prejob health check stops a black hole node
spec: A top box labelled Job sent to a node by the WLM. An arrow down to a diamond labelled prejob health check passes? Yes arrow goes right to a green box: the job starts on the node. No arrow goes down to a red-outlined box labelled node fails the check, the WLM does not start the job there. From that box an arrow goes left to a box labelled Drain action, BCM reschedules the job onto healthy nodes. From Drain an arrow goes down to a grey box labelled node stays drained until an administrator runs undrain after the fix. Side note near the top: Black Hole Node Syndrome, without the guard, an unhealthy node accepts every job and fails them. Orange highlight on the No path. Monospace for prejob, Drain and undrain, and the two cmsh enable commands listed as a small footer: monitoring setup set ib prejob yes, and wlm use slurm set enableprejob yes.
anchor: ### 10.2 Prejob and postjob health checks, power saving, and `nodecustomizations`
alt: Prejob check decision for a job sent to a node
cap: Prejob check: a node that fails the check is drained, so jobs are rescheduled and do not fail on it, until an administrator undrains it.

name: b09-etcd-odd
title: Why etcd uses an odd number of nodes
spec: Two horizontal rows side by side for comparison. Row 1 labelled 3 etcd nodes: three small circles labelled etcd, one crossed out as failed, two remaining with a green tick, text beside: quorum holds, survives one failure. Row 2 labelled 4 etcd nodes: four small circles labelled etcd, one crossed out as failed, three remaining with a green tick, text beside: survives one failure, the extra node adds cost and coordination work. A bracket under both rows with the heading: the same tolerance for one failure. Orange highlight on the extra fourth node in row 2 with the note: adds no failure tolerance. Small monospace label for etcd. A grey note at the bottom: quorum is the majority of members that must agree before a change is saved.
anchor: ## 1. The reference architecture (4.1)
alt: Three and four etcd nodes compared
cap: Odd etcd count: four nodes tolerate no more failures than three, so the extra node adds cost without adding safety.

name: b09-worker-upgrade
title: Order of a Kubernetes upgrade across control plane and workers
spec: A top-to-bottom flow in two lanes. Top lane labelled control plane nodes: box 1 first control plane node: kubeadm upgrade plan, then kubeadm upgrade apply version. Box 2: other control plane nodes: kubeadm upgrade node. Arrow down to the bottom lane. Bottom lane labelled worker nodes, one at a time, with a repeating loop of six small boxes in order: kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets, imageupdate -w --wait, kubeadm upgrade node, systemctl daemon-reload, systemctl restart kubelet, kubectl uncordon. A loop arrow back from the last box to the first labelled next worker. At the end a box: update the Kubernetes version recorded in BCM, because BCM does not update that record itself. Orange highlight on the imageupdate box with the note: update the image too, or a reboot brings back the old version. Monospace for all the commands.
anchor: ## 8. Upgrades, Edge, and Cluster API (CAPI)
alt: Order of a Kubernetes upgrade
cap: Kubernetes upgrade: upgrade the control plane first, then drain, update and uncordon each worker one at a time.

name: b10-docker-escalation
title: How docker group membership becomes root on the node
spec: A left-to-right flow of four boxes with arrows. Box 1: A user in the docker UNIX group. Arrow labelled talks to the socket. Box 2: /var/run/docker.sock, a socket file, the docker CLI sends REST calls to dockerd. Arrow labelled dockerd runs as root on the host. Box 3: dockerd on the host, running as root. Arrow labelled starts a container with the host disk mounted. Box 4 (orange): a container with the host root filesystem mounted at /host, a shell inside it, unrestricted root on the compute node. Below box 4, a grey note line: a Slurm job cancelled with scancel can leave a container running as an orphan that holds GPU memory. Monospace for docker run -v /:/host -it ubuntu chroot /host bash, /var/run/docker.sock and dockerd.
anchor: ### 7.1 Deep dive: Why Docker is an anti-pattern for multi-tenant HPC and Slurm jobs
alt: How the docker socket gives root on the node
cap: Docker escalation: membership in the docker group reaches the root daemon, so any user can mount the host disk.

name: b10-sqsh-prestage
title: Pre-import once, then every node reads the same file
spec: Two rows for comparison. Top row labelled Pulling at job start: 64 nodes in a column each with an arrow going through one narrow box labelled NAT gateway or corporate proxy to the external registry nvcr.io or Docker Hub. Under the arrows a note: 64 times 20 GB is 1.28 TB through the border link. Bottom row labelled Pre-staged: one box enroot import docker://nvcr.io#nvidia/pytorch:24.01-py3 run once on a login or build node, arrow to a single file nvidia+pytorch+24.01-py3.sqsh on parallel storage, then 64 small arrows from the file to the nodes, each node unpacking into local NVMe. Orange highlight on the single .sqsh file with the note: the registry is contacted once. Monospace for the commands and the file name. Caption area note: srun --container-image=/scratch/containers/nvidia+pytorch+24.01-py3.sqsh.
anchor: ### 7.2 Architecting container image caching and registry tiers for 512-GPU jobs
alt: Pulling an image per node versus pre-importing one file
cap: Pre-staged image: import once to shared storage, so 64 nodes read one file instead of pulling from the registry.

name: b11-trigger-timeline
title: Which launch option fires on which sample
spec: A horizontal timeline of consecutive samples drawn as dots on a line, labelled sample 1, sample 2, sample 3 and so on to sample 6 from left to right. A horizontal dashed threshold line across the middle labelled zone: value above 50 (the zone is above the line). Sample dots: sample 1 below the line (outside the zone), sample 2 above (inside), sample 3 above (inside), sample 4 above (inside), sample 5 below (outside), sample 6 above again (inside). Above the timeline, labelled markers: at sample 2, Enter fires, with the note: in the zone and the previous sample was not. Under the timeline, a bracket across samples 3 and 4 labelled During fires on each sample that stays in the zone. At sample 5 a marker Leave fires, with the note: out of the zone after being in it. Sample 1 has a grey note: the first sample can never fire Enter. Orange highlight on the Enter marker. Monospace for Enter, During, Leave.
anchor: ## 4. Triggers: exactly when does it fire? (10.4.5)
alt: Enter, During and Leave on a series of samples
cap: Trigger timing: Enter fires on the first sample in the zone, During on each sample that stays there, and Leave when the value drops out.

name: b11-remediation-tiers
title: Choosing the remediation tier before the action
spec: A top box labelled New alert on a node, with an arrow down to a diamond labelled what kind of fault? Three branches from the diamond to three columns. Column 1 (red-outlined, the most careful): Tier 1, suspected hardware (GPU falls off the bus, uncorrectable ECC, PSU). Action: Drain, notify, collect evidence NVSMHealthDump. A crossed-out box: no automatic reboot or image update. Column 2 (green): Tier 2, reproducible software state (missing mount, wrong package, bad module). Action: Drain, ImageUpdate or reboot, re-run the check, Undrain on PASS. Below it a loop-cap box: after the second failure, move the node to Tier 1. Column 3 (grey): Tier 3, transient (brief fabric blip, one timeout). Action: alert first, use flapping and UNKNOWN, drain only if it persists. Orange highlight on the crossed-out reboot box. Monospace for NVSMHealthDump, ImageUpdate, PASS and Undrain.
anchor: ## 8. Automatic remediation: a design that cannot make things worse
alt: Three remediation tiers by fault type
cap: Remediation tiers: hardware faults are drained and investigated, software faults are repaired from the image, and transient faults get an alert first.

name: b12-failover-timeline
title: A head-node failover from the crash to ACTIVE
spec: A horizontal timeline with time markers on the axis: T equals 0 s, T equals 1 to 5 s, T equals 5 s, T equals 10 s, then a later segment for the quorum window, then BECOMEACTIVE, then ACTIVE. Above the axis at T equals 0 s: head1 panics, the kernel halts. Below the axis: a bracket from 0 to 10 s, the passive head head2 polls head1 once a second over internalnet ping, failoverping and status on port 8081. At T equals 5 s a small warning marker: Warn time, head1 has stopped answering. At T equals 10 s a marker Dead time: head2 moves to FENCING and starts the quorum poll, a window of Quorum time 60 s. Next a marker STONITH: head2 powers off head1 through its BMC or PDU, then polls power status until OFF. Next marker BECOMEACTIVE: prefailover script, mount script for shared NAS, shared internal and external virtual IPs come up, gratuitous ARP sent. Last marker ACTIVE: nfs-server, slurmdbd and the User Portal start. A green side note at T equals 0 s: running Slurm and Kubernetes jobs keep running on the compute nodes. Orange highlight on the STONITH marker with the note: no proof of power-off, no failover. Monospace for FENCING, FENCING, BECOMEACTIVE, ACTIVE, and the commands.
anchor: ### 10.1 Deep dive: Anatomy of a head-node failover from second `0` to `ACTIVE`
alt: Timeline of a head-node failover
cap: Failover timeline: the passive head waits for dead time and quorum, proves the old head is off, then takes over the shared storage and addresses.

name: b12-failover-decision
title: What the passive head does for each kind of outage
spec: A top box labelled Active head stops answering, with a decision chain going down. Diamond 1: Are ping, failoverping and status all NOT OK? No branch goes right to a grey box: mostly dead, alert the administrator, no automatic action, failover by hand with cmha makeactive. Yes branch goes down to Diamond 2: Does power control work, and is disableautomaticfailover no? No branch goes right to a grey box: manual failover, administrator confirms the old head is off. Yes branch goes down to Diamond 3: Does quorum confirm that more than half the nodes cannot reach the active head? No branch goes right to a box: no STONITH, stop. Yes branch goes down to a green box: STONITH powers off the active head, power status shows OFF, then BECOMEACTIVE. Side panel labelled not failovers: a graceful reboot or shutdown of the active head is treated as intentional, use cmha makeactive on the passive head. Orange highlight on the STONITH green box. Monospace for ping, failoverping, status, cmha makeactive and disableautomaticfailover.
anchor: ## 5. Automatic or manual failover
alt: Decision path for head failover
cap: Failover decision: automatic failover needs all three checks down, working power control and quorum, otherwise an administrator decides.

name: b13-rollout-patterns
title: Two rollout patterns: in-place sync or category switch
spec: Two horizontal lanes, each a left-to-right flow, stacked. Top lane labelled Pattern A: user-space updates, no kernel reboot needed. Boxes in order: 1 clone the production image, 2 lock the image and update it in a chroot, 3 updateprovisioners, 4 imageupdate -n node001 dry run and synclog, 5 imageupdate -n node001 -w on the canary, 6 roll out in waves. Bottom lane labelled Pattern B: kernel, driver and OFED changes, reboot needed. Boxes in order: 1 clone the production image to a v2 image and make the kernel and driver updates there, 2 create a canary category pointing at the v2 image and reboot one idle node, 3 validate GPUDirect RDMA and all_reduce_perf, 4 point the production category at v2, 5 chained drain: powerreset then undrain across nodes. A side note on the bottom lane in grey: no in-place sync on a running node, the loaded kernel modules and files on disk would no longer match. Orange highlight on the box that says imageupdate -w in the top lane's step 5 with the note: never use -w for kernel or driver changes. Monospace for commands.
anchor: ### 10.1 Deep dive: Managing software-image lifecycles without breaking running jobs
alt: Two rollout patterns for image changes
cap: Rollout patterns: user-space changes sync in place after a canary, while kernel and driver changes switch the category and reboot nodes.

name: b13-dr-bundle
title: What goes in the off-cluster recovery bundle
spec: Five boxes arranged in a row on the left, each labelled with a number and an item: 1 the latest CMDaemon MySQL dump, plus slurm_acct_db, Keycloak and Harbor databases. 2 images: tarballs or rsync mirrors of /cm/images and /cm/node-installer. 3 configuration outside the database: cmd.conf, named.conf.include, excludelistnormal, excludelistfailover, custom scripts, TLS and CA keys. 4 the BCM license file and its bound head-node MAC addresses. 5 the written Day-0 installation parameters: topology, subnets with IP offsets, disk layout XMLs. All five arrows flow to one large box on the right labelled external backup target, with the note: outside the cluster's own /cm/shared NAS. Below the target box, a green box: rehearse a restore in a lab, for example gunzip of the dump into mysql. Orange highlight on box 4 with the note: a restore onto different hardware can fail the license check. Monospace for file paths and the commands.
anchor: ### 10.2 End-to-end bare-metal disaster recovery rehearsal
alt: Five items in an off-cluster recovery bundle
cap: Recovery bundle: five kinds of artifact, stored off the cluster, are what a rebuild needs.

name: b14-install-order
title: The order of the air-gapped install on the active head node
spec: A top-to-bottom flow of nine numbered boxes with arrows between them, in a single column, each box one step with a short monospace command or action. Step 1: Generate the configuration, cm-kubernetes-setup --airgap-registry master.cm.cluster:5000 --airgap-registry-as-helm, choose save, do not deploy. Step 2: Extract the bundle, on Ubuntu extract under /tmp, not /root. Step 3: cm-kubernetes-setup --airgap-install-system-packages, active head only. Step 4: cm-container-registry-setup --skip-packages, then trust the registry CA with update-ca-certificates. Step 5: Docker, cm-docker-setup --skip-packages, only for Run:ai. Step 6: Push content, --airgap-push-container-images, then --airgap-push-helm-charts. Step 7: extract the CRDs with extract_crds.sh. Step 8: Deploy, cm-kubernetes-setup -c /root/cm-kubernetes-setup.conf. Step 9: Run:ai is deployed afterwards by cm-runai-setup. Orange highlight on step 3 with the note: run on the active head only, never on the passive head, never with --force. Monospace for all commands.
anchor: ## 5. Installing on the air-gapped head node
alt: Ordered steps of the air-gapped install
cap: Air-gapped install order: save the configuration, install packages, trust the registry, push content, then deploy.

name: b14-skew-hops
title: Two hops from 1.33 to 1.35 under the skew rule
spec: A left-to-right sequence of three version boxes connected by two arrows. Box 1: cluster on 1.33. Arrow 1 labelled hop 1, using the 1.34 bundle, with a checklist note: all nodes upgraded and healthy before starting the next hop. Box 2: cluster on 1.34. Arrow 2 labelled hop 2, using the 1.35 bundle. Box 3: cluster on 1.35. Above the arrows a bracket with the rule: at most two adjacent minor versions at any time, and no skipping minors. Under the diagram a small grey comparison: 1.33, 1.34 and 1.35 together is not allowed. Orange highlight on the 1.34 box as the stop point in between. Each hop note: control plane first, one node at a time, then workers in drained batches. Monospace for version numbers 1.33, 1.34, 1.35.
anchor: ### 9.2 Planning multi-hop air-gapped Kubernetes upgrades under the skew policy
alt: Two upgrade hops across Kubernetes minors
cap: Multi-hop upgrade: a cluster on 1.33 reaches 1.35 through an intermediate 1.34 hop, because minors cannot be skipped.

name: b15-psu-feeds
title: Why PSU feed wiring decides how many servers a feed loss takes
spec: Two side-by-side panels for comparison. Left panel titled Interleaved 3 plus 3, not recommended: a DGX B200 server drawn as a box with six small PSU squares, three wired to Feed A (PDU A) and three to Feed B (PDU B). Below, a red cross on PDU A with the note: one PDU fails, 3 of 6 PSUs remain, below the 5 needed, the server goes down, and every server in the rack does too. Right panel titled 6 to make 5: the same server with six PSU squares, each wired to its own independent feed, six separate feed boxes shown along the bottom. A single feed marked failed with a cross, with the note: 5 of 6 PSUs stay energized, the server keeps running. Orange highlight on the left panel's cross, with the note: never wire 3 plus 3. Monospace for PDU A, PDU B, 5 of 6 and 6 to make 5.
anchor: ## 5. Power and cooling: the DGX B200 numbers
alt: Interleaved and six-to-make-five PSU wiring
cap: PSU feeds: a DGX B200 needs five of six supplies, so an interleaved split loses the whole server on one feed failure.

name: b16-checkpoint-loss
title: How much work a failure costs between checkpoints
spec: A horizontal timeline of training steps with labelled markers. Checkpoints saved every 500 steps shown as small tick marks labelled checkpoint interval 500 steps. Marker at step 5000: latest valid checkpoint, loaded after restart. Marker at step 5243: failure hits. Marker at step 5001: first step executed after resume. A bracket between step 5000 and step 5243 labelled steps lost to failure: 5243 minus 5000 equals 243. A dashed lighter segment after 5243 running up to the next checkpoint at step 5500, labelled worst case: a failure just before the next checkpoint loses nearly the whole interval, at most 500 steps. Under the timeline a note: the restart restarts all ranks from the latest complete sharded checkpoint. Orange highlight on the failure marker at step 5243. Monospace for the step numbers and the 500-step interval.
anchor: ### 2.4 How this connects to BCM monitoring and training checkpoints
alt: Steps lost between checkpoints when a failure hits
cap: Checkpoint loss: a failure at step 5243 with checkpoints every 500 steps loses 243 steps, and at most 500 in the worst case.

name: b16-mc-roles
title: The five Mission Control roles and how they relate
spec: Five equal panels in one row or a grid, each a rounded box with a title and a short role line, with NO arrows and NO ordering implied (the source says the roles have no strict order). Panel 1: System health and diagnostics, the foundational health base, tracks system health and hardware status. Panel 2: Telemetry and Observability, proprietary diagnostic tools and health checks surface cluster-wide telemetry. Panel 3: Validation and Diagnostics, supports the autonomous recovery engine for rapid failure recovery. Panel 4: Cluster management operations, BCM and NMX Manager, provisioning and fabric control. Panel 5: Workload orchestration, Slurm, Kubernetes and Run:ai, scheduler access for AI and HPC workloads. Orange highlight on the Validation and Diagnostics panel with the note: the autonomous recovery engine sits here. Monospace for BCM, NMX Manager, Slurm, Kubernetes and Run:ai. A bracket above the row labelled NVIDIA Mission Control: five roles.
anchor: ### 1.1 The Mission Control software stack on a DGX SuperPOD
alt: Five roles in the Mission Control stack
cap: Mission Control stack: health sits at the base, recovery and telemetry above it, then cluster management and workload orchestration.
